title: De Institutione Divinarum Litterarum
author: Cassiodorus

passages.original: Nec non et Epiphanius Cyprius Salaminae Ecclesiae multa eum detestatione persequitur, cum dolore maximo dicta ipsius iniquissima calliditate perversa, pontificis auctoritate redarguens. Sed quemadmodum legi de- beat, in epistola quam 540 scripsit ad Tranquillum sanctus Hieronymus (Epist. 76), probabiliter indica- vit; ut nec studiosos ab ejus necessaria lectione re- moveat, nec iterum incautos praecipitet ad ruinam. Quem quidam non immerito more anethi habendum esse dixerunt, qui dum sacrarum condiat pulmentaria litterarum, ipse tamen decoctus exsuccatusque pro- jicitur.
passages.english: Epiphanius of Cyprus, [bishop] of the church of Salamis, also assails him with much detestation, refuting with the greatest grief and with a bishop's authority his statements, perverted by most wicked cunning. But how he ought to be read, Saint Jerome has plausibly indicated in the letter which he wrote to Tranquillus (Epist. 76), so as neither to keep the studious from the necessary reading of him, nor again to hurl the incautious headlong to ruin. Some have said, not undeservedly, that he should be treated in the manner of dill, which, while it seasons the dishes of sacred letters, is itself nevertheless thrown away once boiled down and drained of its juice.
passages.notes: The number '540' in the text is a page or column marker from the printed edition and has been omitted.

passages.original: In secundo Regum codice, quoniam continui textus expositionem reperire non potui, quaedam frusta disertissimorum virorum, velut in uno quodam vesti- mento contexui, ut membratim possit adunata colle- ctione cognosci, quod sub uno corpore nequaquam potuit inveniri. Primi siquidem voluminis quatuor homilias Origenis inveni. De quo libro etiam beatus Augustinus ad Simplicianum episcopum Mediolanen- sem scribens, sex solvit propositas quaestiones. Qua- rum prima est de loco ubi ait : Et insiluit Spiritus Domini malus in Saul (I Reg.XVI, 10). Secunda vero quaestio est ejusdem libri, quomodo dictum sit : Poe- nitet me quod constituerim regem Saul (I Reg.XV, 11).
passages.english: For the second codex of Kings, since I could not find an exposition of the continuous text, I have woven together certain fragments of most learned men, as if into a single garment, so that what could by no means be found in one body may be learned piece by piece from a collection joined together. For of the first volume I found four homilies of Origen. On this book also the blessed Augustine, writing to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, solved six questions put to him. The first of these is on the passage where it says: "And an evil spirit of the Lord leapt upon Saul" (1 Kings 16:10). The second question, from the same book, is how it was said: "I repent that I have made Saul king" (1 Kings 15:11).
passages.notes: 'Kings' follows the Vulgate numbering, where 1–2 Kings correspond to 1–2 Samuel.

passages.original: De quo libro etiam memoratus sanctus Hieronymus ad Vitalem scripsit episcopum (Epist. 132); quomodo Salomon et Achaz, cum essent in undecimis annorum curriculis constituti, filios genuisse dicantur, quod natura minime probatur habere communis. Nam et sanctus Augustinus in libro Civitatis Dei decimo se- ptimo, titulo quarto, dum inter alia de Regum tem- poribus facundissimus disputator eloquitur, canticum Annae dilucidavit ex ordine.
passages.english: On this book also the aforementioned Saint Jerome wrote to Bishop Vitalis (Epist. 132), [explaining] how Solomon and Ahaz are said to have begotten sons when they were in the eleventh year of their lives, which common nature is by no means shown to allow. For Saint Augustine too, in the seventeenth book of The City of God, chapter four, while, as a most eloquent disputant, he speaks among other things of the times of the Kings, explained the song of Hannah in order.

passages.original: Itemque Daniel (licet apud Hebraeos nequaquam prophetico choro recipitur, sed inter eos annumeratur qui Hagiographa conscripserunt) tribus libris a supra memorato sancto Hieronymo noscitur explanatus. Residuos vero duodecim prophetas. quos vulgus [ed., sermo vulgaris] propter brevita- tem librorum suorum minores appellat, viginti li- bris supradictus sanctus Hieronymus commentatus esse dignoscitur : id est, Osee libris tribus, Abdiam libro uno, Amos libris tribus, Joel libro uno, Jonam libro uno, Nahum libro uno, Habacuc libris duobus, Sophoniam libro uno, Aggaeum libro uno, Zachariam libris tribus, Michaeam libris duobus, Malachiam li- bro uno.
passages.english: Likewise Daniel (although among the Hebrews he is by no means received into the prophetic choir, but is counted among those who wrote the Hagiographa) is known to have been expounded in three books by the above-mentioned Saint Jerome. The remaining twelve prophets, whom the common people [ed.: common speech] call minor because of the brevity of their books, the aforesaid Saint Jerome is recognized to have commented on in twenty books: that is, Hosea in three books, Obadiah in one book, Amos in three books, Joel in one book, Jonah in one book, Nahum in one book, Habakkuk in two books, Zephaniah in one book, Haggai in one book, Zechariah in three books, Micah in two books, Malachi in one book.
passages.notes: The bracketed variant 'sermo vulgaris' is the edition's note, kept as given.

passages.original: ut simul omnes legentibus offerantur, qui tractatores unius voluminis exstiterunt. Unde etiam et sanctus Ambrosius in libro tertio Patriar- charum, ubi de persona Isaac loquitur, multa salu- briter luculenterque disseruit. Saepe dictus autem Pater Hieronymus asserit Sapientiae librum, non a Salomone (ut usus habet), sed a Philone doctissimo quodam Judaeo fuisse conscriptum, quem pseudogra- plium praenotavit, propterea quod usurpationem no- minis portat alterius. Cujus voluminis expositionem presbyter Bellator octo libris se assumpsisse testatus est, quem cum aliis opusculis ejus pariter sustinemus.
passages.english: so that all who were commentators on a single volume might be offered to readers together. Hence also Saint Ambrose, in the third book of the Patriarchs, where he speaks of the person of Isaac, discussed many things wholesomely and clearly. The often-mentioned Father Jerome asserts that the book of Wisdom was written not by Solomon (as custom holds) but by Philo, a most learned Jew, and he labelled it pseudepigraphal, because it bears the usurpation of another's name. The priest Bellator has testified that he undertook an exposition of this volume in eight books, which we await together with his other works.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence. 'pseudographum' read for the scanned 'pseudogra- plium'. The reference to Ambrose's 'third book of the Patriarchs' is unclear; the work meant may be his treatise on Isaac.

passages.english: The division of divine Scripture according to Jerome.
The division of divine Scripture according to Augustine.

passages.original: Multi iterum Patres nostri talibus litteris eruditi,) et in lege Domini permanentes, ad veram sapientiam pervenerunt, sicut beatus Augustinus in libro de Do- ctrina Christiana meminit (Lib.II, cap. 4), dicens : Non aspicimus quanto auro et argento et veste suf- farcinatus exierit de AEgypto Cyprianus, et doctor suavissimus, et martyr beatissimus; quanto Lactan- tius, quanto Victorinus, Optatus, Hilarius; nos ad- dimus Ambrosium, ipsumque Augustinum, atque Hieronymum, multosque alios innumerabiles Graecos. Hoc etiam ipse fidelissimus Dei famulus Moyses fe- cit;
passages.english: Again, many of our Fathers, educated in such letters and abiding in the law of the Lord, attained true wisdom, as the blessed Augustine recalls in the book On Christian Doctrine (Book 2, ch. 4), saying: "Do we not see with how much gold and silver and clothing Cyprian, that most delightful teacher and most blessed martyr, was loaded when he came out of Egypt? How much Lactantius, how much Victorinus, Optatus, Hilary?" We add Ambrose, and Augustine himself, and Jerome, and countless others, Greeks too. This also that most faithful servant of God, Moses, himself did;
passages.notes: The Augustine quotation is rendered as a question ('Do we not see'). The text reads 'Non aspicimus', literally 'we do not see'; the question form assumes the familiar rhetorical sense.

passages.original: Hoc enim nobis est sa- lutare, proficuum, gloriosum, perpetuum, quod [ed., quoniam) nulla mors, nulla mobilitas, nulla possit separare oblivio; sed in illa suavitate patriae, cum Domino faciet aeterna exsultatione gaudere. Quod si alicui fratrum (ut meminit Virgilius)
passages.english: For this is for us saving, profitable, glorious, everlasting, because [ed.: since] no death, no change, no forgetfulness can separate [us from it]; but in that sweetness of the homeland it will make [us] rejoice with the Lord in eternal exultation. But if for any of the brothers (as Virgil recalls)
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-sentence; the following Virgil quotation is not supplied.

passages.original: Quod si hujus studii requirantur auctores, de hor- tis scripsit pulcherrime Gargilius Martialis a, qui et nutrimenta olerum, et virtutes eorum diligenter ex- posuit, ut ex illius commentarii lectione (praestante Domino) unusquisque et saturari valeat et sanari; quem vobis inter alios codices reliqui.
passages.english: But if authors on this pursuit are sought, Gargilius Martialis wrote most beautifully about gardens, and he carefully set out both the cultivation of vegetables and their properties, so that from reading his treatise (the Lord granting) everyone may be able both to be fed and to be healed. I have left him to you among the other codices.
passages.notes: 'nutrimenta olerum' could mean either the cultivation of vegetables or their nourishing value; it is rendered here as cultivation. The 'a' after Martialis is a footnote mark and has been omitted.
